utterances.text: I didn't see him in the region myself. And as for reports, he could have obtained them in Backa Palanka or at any other place. So you wouldn't have to actually go to a flash-point area in order to obtain some information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to be more specific. Do you agree with me that he was a solid professional, who, as far as you could see, was engaged in nothing other than collecting intelligence to put into reports, such as the one we've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree. Operatives have to write many reports, and it is up to their bosses to assess which information has operative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You didn't observe him having any decision-making authority within the RSK; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. I know that he had no decision-making authority because there was a State Security Service of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's return to this document, page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. And there is reference three paragraphs down in English to: "The cause for dismissing the mentioned MUP members is reportedly an incident that has taken place the day before at the border crossing near Tovarnik." Did you know about that border crossing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about it in a report, and it was also visible. When I arrived there, the ramp there was broken. That was something that was kept across the road, and then it would be lifted when somebody needed to pass through. So that was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Kojic engaged in crime prevention activities that border crossing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. There is no mention of Kojic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I know there is not a mention here. I'm asking you if you know whether Kojic was engaged in crime prevention activities at Tovarnik either then or later?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why would an assistant minister take part in border crossing controls? That's something that the unit, the crew, should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which unit, which crew?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border crossing unit which checks all border crossings and which secures -- which is in charge of securing the border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen now P987.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This, you will see, is a letter by -- or from Martic dated 7th of October, 1994, directly to Milosevic; to the prime minister of Serbia, Milanovic; to the minister of the interior, Zoran Sokolovic; and to the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Perisic. And it's entitled: "Subject: Another Incident at the Tovarnik Crossing." And if you just have a look quickly at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we go to the second page of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this letter, as you'll see, is a complaint by Martic, and he is essentially complaining about Kojic and his men and Kostic and his men. Do you see the paragraph which begins: "At the crossing, I was met by Colonel Stojan Spanovic, Corps Chief of Staff ..."?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it that. And I know Stojan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Martic's complaint at this time, complaining that Kojic and Kostic were effectively acting against his interests, including having their men stop him at the Tovarnik crossing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These weren't Kojic's or Kostic's men. This was the check-point unit, and there was an oversight on their part. They did not recognise the minister right away. And when -- for instance, when they would stop me, I would behave like any other participant in traffic. Now, he felt offended that he hadn't been recognised by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But how do you know about this incident; and how do you know that they were not Kojic's or Kostic's men?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the border crossing is run by the police station in the border area. Now, if Kojic and Kostic were to have their own men at each one of the border crossings, and there were 13 of them, do you know what large number of men they would have to have? And that in three shifts on top?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you went through that border crossing in October or thereabouts of 1994, and you saw that these men were not Kojic's or Kostic's men; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were police members in charge of that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Okay. So we're clear about one thing: that they're regular police members. Nothing to do with a paramilitary force. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that Martic was writing to Milosevic accusing Kojic and Kostic of things that they hadn't done?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. As for this, I know that he was very offended. But I could also give you an opposite example. However, the Trial Chamber wants me to be to the point and succinct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, in your last question, you asked for a reason for accusing someone of which he hadn't done. Now, that's a rather composite question, isn't it. If you say, "I do not," that may be understood as an implicit affirmation of that he hadn't done any of the thing. It could also be limited to not knowing the reasons. So this type of questions and the answer you can expect is at a risk to create confusion rather than to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you please avoid that type of confusing answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- let me try to deal with it in a different way. Page 4 of the English, please, and I hope it's going to be 4 of the B/C/S. And the paragraph I'm interested in: "Mr. President of the Republic, Mr. Prime Minister, Minister of the Interior, Chief of Staff ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 2 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the paragraph notes: "Mr. President of the Republic, Mr. Prime Minister, Minister of the Interior, Chief of Staff, my decision at present is not to go public with everything that happens to me in the state of which I am the president. There is overwhelming evidence that the state security of the MUP of Serbia is behind these paramilitary and parapolice forces." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I know of this incident. I know of it, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I'm interested in is whether you know, or knew at the time, that Martic - like Arkan before - was suspicious, paranoid about the DB, the Serbian DB and its influence within the RSK? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether he was paranoid. All I know is that in higher education, at the college that he attended, his average grade was 1.9 in Zagreb. And you earn that kind of grade when you actually have to retake an exam a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just simplify it. Do you know anything about Martic's view towards the Serbian DB in -- and particularly Jovica Stanisic, in 1994, going into 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Martic thought that he was above everyone else in Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you know nothing specific about the DB? Yes or no, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 65 ter 1D02572, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to move onto 1995 and issues surrounding the 11th Corps. This is a document written by an operative. It's a report by an operative of the RDB Novi Sad. And I just want to ask you if can you confirm some of the details in it. First of all, the first paragraph notes that the corps, the 11th Corps, had about 21.000 men. Do you know if that's correct, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thousand more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 22.000, you think?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, moving through the document, trying to save some time, if we can go to page 3 of the English and 2 of the B/C/S. And it says there halfway down the page in the English: "Until recently, a battalion of special forces operated independently in providing security at the oil wells in Dzeletovci, the so-called Boca's Battalion. However, according to the latest information, this battalion has placed itself fully under the corps' command." Do you know if that was -- is correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, that means that the witness has considered every part of what is written here, where he says it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me break it down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Such as that, until recently, special forces operated independently. I mean, it's a lot of information --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and I'd like to be sure that I understand the answer in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me break that down, Mr. Witness. If you can try to limit your answers and, if possible, answer yes or no and give an explanation only when strictly necessary, because my time is running quickly. In June of 1995, when this document was written, were you aware that Boca's Battalion had placed itself fully under the 11th Corps command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know whether, from that point onwards, Boca's Battalion received its supplies from the 11th Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But still a part of the oil industry, which in 1995 was still using the raw crude oil.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to page 5 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S. And we have there a paragraph which says: "Apart from the army, in the event of Croatia's aggression, the detachment of the PJM of the SUP of Beli Manastir would also be included in the defence and would be attached to the 60th Brigade for anti-landing and anti-sabotage activities. According to establishment, the detachment is part of the brigade and is based in Erdut. It is made up of active-duty and reserve police officers out. Were you aware, Mr. Djukic, of a detachment of police officers, PJM, based in Erdut in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that. This was still the unit in Erdut, but because of the incursion of the Ustashas to Kopacki Rit we dislocated or removed 60 people into a separate unit. I even have a photograph showing their success in liquidating the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at the same time as this detachment of PJM was based in Erdut, the Ministry of Defence was also based in Erdut; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a small distance away. It's a castle. And this was actually the centre of pre-military training in -- just in front of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were the Ministry of Defence in Erdut responsible, in part, for sending units of the 11th Corps on operations within the RSK? Men were sent from Erdut; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would kindly ask you to repeat your question. I don't know how they would be going from the RSK to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. We have to talk about military terminology a little bit and get into that if we're going to talk about the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let me try to break it down. The Ministry of Defence in Erdut, do you know what its responsibilities were, in brief?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, it was exclusively equipping the units, providing food, weapons, and other materiel and logistical support issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I please have information about provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll send that, Your Honour, right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So maybe it could be MFI'd, Your Honour, until we receive that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar the number to be assigned to the document would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D764, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D764 is marked for identification, under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to some further documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I have on the screen, please, 1D05455 and ERN number 0415 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. 1D05455, ERN 04150670.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The subject I want to the ask you about is your knowledge of troop -- troops being sent from the 11th Corps in 1994 and 1995 to the Republika Srpska, whether you have knowledge of some of these issues.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let me see if you do. This is an intercept of a conversation. Have a look at it and see if can you assist with any issue. Or let me ask you a question once you've read it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This, it suggests, that Loncar had direct command in November of 1994 of the -- of Boca. Would you agree with that, that he did?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a degree. Because already it arises from previous documents, and we've already talked about it - and from statements by Mrgud himself - that both of them had authority over that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. This -- the document I think is more accurately described as a summary of an intercept rather than an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to make a similar observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document that I'm interested in you looking at, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D05293. ERN -- sorry, 1D05293. Fortunately, I can see the frustrated stenographer. ERN 04150678. And it's B/C/S page 5, English page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the previous document, the draft translation gives a date, whereas the original bears no date. May I take it that it's taken from the context of a series of summaries or?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll have to check that. I'm not altogether sure. We hadn't spotted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's pretty obvious. And, as a matter of fact, for the present document, we have the same problem. It gives a time, it gives a number, but, apparently, there's no date in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I check this while we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You see there, summary of an intercept in front of you on the screen. "General Dusan Loncar, commander of the 11th Corps, who is on the battle-field in western Bosnia, will return to Vukovar on the 20th of November, 1994, along with the military that is currently on the battle-field there."

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That does correspond to the time, judging by what I know that my police members were killed on the 10th and the 11th. That would indicate that Loncar returned around the 11th. But I did not actually have any oversight as to where he was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your police members were killed on the 10th and the 11th. But where were they killed, and what were they doing when they were killed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kordun, defending the 5th Corps. Dudakovic was in jeopardy by the attempt of independence of western Bosnia, under the leadership of Fikret Abdic and his newly formed forces. And it suited us more to keep Fikret where he was, because he was open for co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So why -- why was it that police officers -- no, let me start that again. Were units of police officers, then, being sent to assist Fikret Abdic in 1994 alongside members of the 11th Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's just that I don't know what zone they were active in. They were led by General Mile Novakovic. I was not involved in that military operation. The late Kostic was in charge, and he did not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So would you agree with this - and we'll look at some more intercepts - but throughout -- from the end -- throughout 1994 and into 1995, units of the 11th Corps were being sent to assist Fikret Abdic, as were a number of police units being sent from the RSK to assist Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Slavonia and Baranja area, I know of this case that you talked about, about the return of Loncar on the 20th of November. Perhaps from other regions, Lika, Knin, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if men were being sent on a regular basis from Erdut to assist Fikret Abdic in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, you don't know; or yes, you do know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not sent on a regular basis. I said that. What does regular mean? It would mean on the basis of shifts. Then you would have one company go from the 1st to the 15th, and then another from the 15th until the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is that what happened? They went on the basis of shifts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly. Not on a continual basis for our units always to have been there, to have had a presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And they were being organised in Erdut; is that right? Was it -- the Ministry of Defence organising them in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The unit was based in Erdut all the time. If you're thinking about the special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How big was the special police unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot say that. I said that when I was answering about the arrival of the police from Serbia. The unit had 100 to 1.000 people. The needed number was taken from the regular forces. For example, the Tovarnik police station, 90 people; 40 would go for an assignment and the remaining 50 would have to increase their number of work hours in order to be able to make up this final number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that, for example, if 80 men from the special police unit were sent from Erdut to assist Fikret Abdic, then you, as police officer, might need further reinforcements while those 80 men were in the operations assisting Fikret Abdic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We wouldn't need reinforcements for that number outside of our area. We never asked for reinforcements from Serbia. Our units did not only go to Kordun. They also went to Okucani in batches of 150 men until Okucani fell on the 2nd of May, 1995. Also Knin, Benkovac, where there were much -- many fewer people in relation to the actual space. The density of our population was the highest in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at 1D05293.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's 1D05293. Oh, it's already on. And it's English page 14 and B/C/S page 14. And Your Honour, before this moves on, if one takes -- moves the B/C/S to the left of the document on the screen, you can see the date. I think that's -- yep, there it is. And the ERN number we want now is 0415 to 0734.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Dated the 18th of December, 1994. And it notes: "From the interview of General Loncar, with some Mica from General Staff of SVK, we learn: In the last tour, 460 soldiers from the 11th Corps went to Bihac battle-field. Next change, shift of about 400 soldiers' strength should enter the Bihac battle-field on the 21st of December." Is that description consistent with your understanding of what was happening within the 11th Corps in December of 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's wrong with the number?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number, and I will tell you the reason. The number of people could have come from the 21st Corps that was covering Kordun with Loncar just being in charge, because it doesn't say here which corps was giving how many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have a date, a translation of the time, which seems to be not corresponding to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. It looks as though the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks as if it is 15:04:00, whereas in the English it looks as if it is 14:04:00. Or are my eyes getting worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I think your eyes -- yeah. Your eyes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, may -- that one hour of difference may not make a great difference, but I'm always concerned about the accuracy of these type of translations. If such simple mistakes are already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apologies. We'll rectify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move onto some more intercepts and see if you can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D05293. English, page 10; B/C/S, page 10. ERN 04150725. 11th December, 1994. 19:22:00. Let's just have a look at this: "NS of the 11th Corps Colonel Spanovic, informs General Loncar that they have failed to persuade members of the Battalion of 45th Brigade from Bijelo Brdo to go to Bihac battle-field so the personnel from the battalion of 45th Brigade from Mirkovci will go in this tour." Do you know anything about men, these men or any other military men going from Mirkovci to the Bihac battle-field in December of 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. Nobody told me that I would be testifying about this topic. I don't have General Loncar's war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, no one is going to blame you if you can't answer and you don't know. No witness knows everything. If you can, please assist, and if you can't, no problem. Do you know anything about the 45th Brigade being located in Mirkovci?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about them being sent at any time to the Bihac battle-field, whether in 1994 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we take a break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break. Could you tell us how much time you would need after the break, because you used until -- you said up to two hours you would need. You are coming close to two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Ideally, I would like 30 minutes because I still have some intercepts to go through, but if I could ask for 20 that would be really useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes are granted after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please verify that the language of what you call intercepts, or summary of intercepts, even suggests such, we learned that, that is not the usual language you would find even in a summary of an intercept. Could you please verify it carefully where it stems from and -- because it's -- I'm a bit puzzled by the language used here and there. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 1.00. And then you have until 1.00, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you have until five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Djukic, if you can try to keep your answers as short as possible, and I'll try to make my questions as specific as possible so we can get through a few more intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen 1D05293 B/C/S page 16; English, page 17. ERN 04150736. And it's a summary of an intercept, 19th of December, 1994 from the conversation between General Loncar and an unidentified other participant in the General Staff of the VSK. I highlight the following: "Loncar has recently sent a request to General Staff SVK asking for the delivery of some fuel that he needs. However, it was not delivered because there no fuel, not even there. The shortage of fuel jeopardizes the sending of a shift to the Bihac front. Loncar states that for the shift accomplishment he uses 15 buses and pays for 8 t of fuel. Namely, he can engage five buses while the rest he gets from Auto-trans from Sid and from Backa Palanka, and he pays with 21 of D2 for 1 kilometre." Simple question, Mr. Djukic. Were you aware that Loncar arranged for the fuel to transport members of the 11th Corps to the Bihac region in December of 1994 and into 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that the RSK had agreement with the Republika Srpska in relation to supplying operations assisting Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that agreement involved the RSK providing those assisting Fikret Abdic with fuel, logistics, and ammunition, through 1994 and into 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their logistics arrangements were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let's go to another intercept. 1D05293, please. B/C/S, page 18; English, page 19. ERN 04150743. Date 24th of December 1994. "General Loncar asked from the General Staff of the SVK, even from the president of so-called RSK Milan Martic to intervene by the authorities in so-called FRY to enable the shift of men from the 11th Corps consisting of six full and eight empty buses and to unknown number of trucks and terrain vehicles to cross the territory of so-called FRY to the territory of B and H in the direction of Bihac front." And then further down the page to the second paragraph and the last line: "At 1655, an unknown voice from General Staff SVK was reported to General Loncar that the president had arranged everything, that he could proceed." Were you privy to any information which confirmed that Martic approved and supported the sending police and military units to assist in the Republika Srpska in late 1994, into 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that Martic was kept up to date and fully informed of those transfers of men to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite certain that Loncar never bypassed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D05293. B/C/S -- that's 1D05293, B/C/S page 34; English, page 35. ERN 04150801.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 18th of February, 1995. "From the interview of Colonel Grozdanic, assistant commander for logistics of the 11th Corps, with Milan Milovanovic, Mrgud, former assistant minister of defence. We learn that during the night of the 18th and 19th February, the buses with the soldiers from Baranja Division returning from west Bosnian battlefield should arrive in the zone of the responsibility of the corps. The permission to go through the territory of so-called FRY should obtain Milan Martic, the president of so-called RSK, at the president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic." Now you've -- you earlier said, Mr. Djukic, that you didn't know anything about Martic's fallout and dislike of Stanisic in late 1994. Do you know anything about Martic's direct line to Slobodan Milosevic, in relation to operations in the Bihac region in late 1994/early 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that Martic went occasionally for a consultation with the late Milosevic and that he always sought his opinion and approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you -- are you able to confirm that that was not a relationship which relied upon indirect channels of communication. They had a direct line to each other. Martic could call up Milosevic in relation to these operations in the Bihac region?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fikret would first get in touch with President Milosevic, and then the others would. That was for the original or initial agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as an ongoing operation, are you able to say -- do you have direct or indirect knowledge of Martic contacting Milosevic directly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where is that knowledge from, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know from my conversation with Martic. He would say, I called Sloba, I told Sloba, or Sloba told me. He didn't lie to me. At least not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he continue, Martic, to -- sorry if I've asked this before, but it's important. But in late 1994 and early 1995 when these operations were ongoing, did Martic ever change his view about the Serbian DB? Did he suddenly start to express trust in them, or was he always someone who regarded the likes of Kojic and Kostic as a problem?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot understand that. They were close friends. They spoke on a number of occasions. For instance, when I went to Ilok, sometimes I would even sit at a different table and they would sit at another table, which I didn't mind at all. From what I could observe myself, they had a very good relationship mutually, and he even continued this relation with Kojic when Dalmacija fell. Kojic offered all kinds of assistance to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To who, sorry?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Martic. He even assisted him in Serbia. He attended his daughter's wedding, and I think that to this day he still occasionally visits his family in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. And Kostic. How did Kostic die; do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never learnt. His daughters -- his little daughters asked me, they implored me because he didn't have a son. They had some ideas about how that happened, but these are versions that I wouldn't want to bring out here. But I -- to me, it's a mystery how he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a rumour that Arkan had had something to do with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were rumours that Legija had killed him. But these were just rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to 1D05293, please. B/C/S page 38; English page 39. ERN 04150859.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Date, 29th of March, 1995. "A Colonel Milan (from FRY Belgrade) said that while talking to the General Mladic that he found larger quantities of ammunition cal 7.62-millimetre; namely, 6 million bullets for 2 million deutschemarks. Milan who worked together with the General Bajic says that the staff for the defence of Krajina is formed, so they intend to enlarge it with representatives of RS and they could later form the staff for the defence of RS. The aim of the establishment of these staffs is to gather volunteers and clothes and other MTS for the needs of VRS and SVK."

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's deceit. Martic said that Karadzic would cut deals, that would be the expense of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and this became evident when Western Slavonia was occupied. And I would really appreciate it if you asked me about how that happened. Please ask me how Western Slavonia fell. And if you don't have -- if you -- unless you've planned to ask me about that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask you, but I'll -- forgive me if I don't. Let ask you about one more intercepts and then I'm almost done. Let me just stick with this intercept for a moment though. Is this, as described here, an illustration of the supply arrangement between the RSK -- or let me put it differently, between the VRS and the SVK in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. While I was in logistics, we paid for certain ammunition and other materiel with cattle or grain and similar items. As to how this was done, I really don't know. And I'm referring to Posavina, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to 1D05293. B/C/S page 25; and English page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I won't read it to save time, but just read that to yourself. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Radojcic was a neighbour of mine and a good friend, and I believe that in the past days, or these days, he was -- has been convicted of war crimes. As for these events, I never learnt about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave that there. Let me just ask you, then, now, quickly about the Erdut Agreement. Do you know anything about the Erdut Agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I do. I was the one who tried to make it happen, and I took part in its drafting. I even drafted some paragraphs, and I believe I have it with me, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the agreement was signed on the 12th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And part of that agreement was that all persons had the right to return freely to their place of residence in the region; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And those who were in place, they were allowed to stay, provided that they vacated the private properties they had taken possession of. So if someone from Daruvar, for instance, was able to pay for rent, under an Article 7 of the Erdut Agreement they would not have to return do their original place of residence, and there were similar incidents such as these -- this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the Erdut agreement was the precursor to the eventual peace agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, was explicit. After long and exhausting negotiations, he said explicitly that he would not sign the agreement. This is the Croatian name for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and pursuant to that agreement, the Security Council of the UN adopted Resolution 1037 that I had occasion with others to implement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: A portion of the witness's answer was not heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just try to clarify this. You talked about Tudjman saying that he explicitly would not sign the agreement --

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the issue of the eastern-most parts of Croatia were resolved. That would be Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem according to us. And in Zagreb they referred to that same area as the Croatian Podunavlje or, rather, the Danube river area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So basically what you are saying is that Tudjman needed to see the Erdut Agreement finalised before he would move onto a wider, more broad peace agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Dayton Agreements were in fact -- had the same concept. However, he placed a condition on it. He wanted to have the resolution of these areas, he wanted that resolved before he would place his signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness mentions the agreement that was a condition for Tudjman to sign the agreement, but I never see -- I haven't seen it in the transcript. Although the witness mentioned the name of the agreement itself twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps could you seek -- apparently something is missing. What was the condition for Tudjman to sign the agreement? Could you tell us, Witness? No, I'm not asking to you find documents. But could you tell us what the condition was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pre-condition was the final resolution of the status of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. In other words, the areas where I was working. Practically that was the only portion of the remaining parts of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The rest had been occupied, or as the Croatians would see it, liberated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, does this meet your concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the witness would only say which agreement it was that was a condition for the resolution of this agreement -- of this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm referring to the Dayton Peace Accords that dealt with the peaceful resolution in all the areas, in all the republics that had been affected by war. In other words, in Bosnia, in Croatia, and the remaining parts of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you are well beyond the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Ilija Kojic play a role in bringing about the Erdut Agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was -- this would be a topic that Serbs would have had some benefit from. He played football together with me and I don't want to be unfair to him. I was -- I had connections with the civilian arm of UNPROFOR in the UNPA area, and that's under Resolution 743 of the Security Council of the United Nations. According to the Vance Plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kojic play a role in bringing about the Erdut Agreement? That was the question. Did he or did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really -- in line 22, on page 69, there's mention made of football. I did not hear the witness saying that in B/C/S. And I believe this is what is causing the misunderstanding in the role of Kojic and the signing of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that he played something together with you. Could you tell us what it was that he played together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The key role. A very important role, if that's easier to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our interpreters are fully capable of interpreting someone who speaks at a speed of speech which is acceptable. Mr. Jordash, a key role. Now you want to explore that key role, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Not explore, but I would like to ask what -- if he could just describe in two sentences what the key role was. That's what I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two sentences for the key role.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, are you able to tell us in two sentences what his key role was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had very good relations, as I've already said, with UNPROFOR and the civilian police of the UNPROFOR which -- which played their role together with their headquarters, and they tried to make this agreement finalised. They interceded with their headquarters in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Kojic was instrumental in that, if I understood you well. Is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, Ms. Marcus will now start her cross-examination. Ms. Marcus is counsel for the Prosecution. And the best way to assist our interpreters is not to adapt your language to what you consider to be their abilities. There's no need for that. The best way to assist them is to speak at such a speed that they are able to do their job as good as they always do. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, Your Honour, asked me to give our position on the admission of D763, MFI, and we have no objection to the admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D763 is admitted into evidence. And was it MFI'd under seal? Not it was not, I think. No, it's a public document. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, please, to respond as briefly as you can, so I don't have to interrupt you in your full answers. If we need any follow-up, we will certainly ask you for it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The Posavina corridor was of great strategic importance to the Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And the reason for this was that the corridor would be the sole route by land between the then-RSK and the municipalities around Banja Luka. In other words, a connection between the Serb-held areas of eastern and western Bosnia and, in fact, the aim was to connect the Krajina through Bosnia to Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Posavina corridor went through Brcko and alongside Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In fact, the establishment of this corridor or a link through Krajina to Serbia linking the Serb-held areas was part of the original six strategic objectives of the Serb authorities, both in Serbia and in Bosnia. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The corridor depended -- existed independently of Banja Luka or Belgrade. There was a motorway there. It's not anything new.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to P1132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there anything in dispute over what we heard of the last two and half, three minutes? Strategic importance being part of the six strategic goals, that it is -- but what was it Brcko alongside Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: None of that is in dispute. The only query that I would raise would be my learned friend's categorisation in the question of the six strategic objectives belonging both to Serbia and Bosnia, and what I was going to ask was that the question be separated so that we're clear what the witness has agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Marcus, there's a request by Mr. Jordash and some guidance from my side as to focus on matters which are in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect to Your Honour's guidance, there will be a piece of evidence which I will raise later directly relating to this which is very much in dispute. So I would just point that out, that this was laying the ground for that later question. With respect to Mr. Jordash's comment, I will indeed break it up and clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, this -- establishment of this corridor as a link between the Serb-held areas, I asked you whether it was part of the original six strategic objectives of the Serb authorities, and I asked you both in Serbia and in Bosnia. What I intended with that last part of the question was to ask you whether you knew that both the Serbian authorities in Serbia, as well as the Bosnian Serb authorities, shared that same strategic objective?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, I think that it is not clear again which question the witness is answering. All of the six goals or one of them? But it's not specified which one of the six he's being asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A corridor between Semberija and the Krajina appears in Adjudicated Fact 155, and therefore I really wonder whether we have to deal with that because that's usually referred to as the Posavina corridor, isn't it? And if you think that the matter remains unclear, you have an opportunity in re-examination, Mr. Petrovic, to clarify. I think matters as they stand now are sufficiently clear. You may proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you served in 1991, you told us, in the Brcko garrison as a military intelligence and security operative. But you also said that you were still officially assigned to Zagreb. So do I understand you correctly, that while you were still officially in a position in the police structures, you were simultaneously, in fact, operating as part of the Brcko JNA garrison as a military intelligence and security operative?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me correctly. I answered precisely to the question from the Defence, that upon my own request I was retired on the 20th of June, 1990. And then from that point on I did not have any responsibilities towards Croatia, in terms of employment or in any other sense. The other question that I clarified is this. If someone was to be deployed in a certain unit, he had to reside and report to the military department, in order to receive his war-time assignment. I received my deregistration from Croatia on the 4th of May, and I -- I took out a new ID card on the 6th of May, and from that point onwards I had nothing to do with Zagreb anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And that new ID card, is that a military or a police ID card, or some other kind of ID card?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it's quite understandable. When I said that I had gone to my place of birth, the village of Cerik, where I registered as a resident and then was issued a personal ID card as a citizen, and it is only on the basis of that personal ID card that I can receive other types of documents in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. So with that personal ID card from your place of birth, you then went and enrolled with the JNA garrison in Brcko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the garrison before. It wasn't a condition for a network of associates --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did that in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "It wasn't a condition for a network of associates...," and what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say anything else. For a person to be able to work at the garrison and to be mobilised, he was required to get an assignment in his military booklet which was co-ordinated with the military department or the barracks or some other kind of military formation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, once you were mobilised, your role in the military structures was that of intelligence and security operative; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the importance of the military booklets in your view, and you told us that those mobilised in January 1992, including some of your relatives, should have their military booklets reflect their mobilisation. Did your military booklet then reflect your mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I need to explain because this was not noted earlier. On that day, on the 16th of January, both my sons were mobilised into the 17th Tactical Group. So we came to Cerik, near Brcko, to war, to defend the place. That's where my own mother was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Djukic. I'm -- what I'm trying to do is to take different pieces of your evidence where you explain your role and just clarify that part, and then we'll go back and talk in more detail about other areas of your evidence. So what I'm asking you now about is your path, your career, police and military path. Now when you gave us some evidence about April 1992 in Bosanski Samac - and, again, I'm just focussing on your position now - you were asked to participate in a meeting regarding the public security station because you, as you said, "should help build up an organisation with all the required material and assets that a public security should have." So, now, in a military intelligence operative capacity, you were asked to advise the police. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That meeting, on the 12th of April, was held in Donji Zabar in the Agroposavina facility, which is much closer to my house than to Bosanski Samac, and my assignment was just to draft a document about the internal organisation and systemisation as a draft which would only become final when it was voted on by the Municipal Assembly of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: But you were -- at the time you were affiliated with the military, not with the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are armed forces. There was no obstacle there. It was just a kind of assistance. And other than that, Samac, Pelagicevo, and Brcko all belonged to the same corps. But an intelligence operative did not have any boundaries as to his area of work. He would go anywhere where the information led him to. But that was not this kind of task. It was a kind of professional type of task and well-meaning assistance that was being offered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, at some point after the takeovers of Bosanski Samac and Brcko but before your injury, you took up duties in the intelligence and security organ in the Bijeljina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was very precise in saying that I was practically permanently employed at the intelligence and security organ of the Eastern Bosnia Corps only from the 17th of November, when I came from Banja Koviljaca Spa for my medical treatment, and then I continued with my treatment in Banja Dvorovi Spa near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Which authority would have possession of your military personnel file; the authorities in Zagreb, the authorities in Bosnia, the authorities in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Brcko. I was residing in Brcko and my military records are in Brcko, but they would always let them know which unit I was in and I was obliged to report to them any changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just so that I understand, does this -- the military activities you undertook with the JNA prior to the breakup, so -- would still be held in Brcko and not in Belgrade. Is that your evidence? The documentation recording your military participation is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say at any point that I lived in Belgrade during the war-time-period, other than during my medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that when you were hospitalised to have the shrapnel removed in February 1993, that you were visited by Martic and Kostic. Martic suggested you could help in the ministry and that, if necessary, he would take this up with President Karadzic. Now I'm asking you specifically still about your positions, your -- your path, in terms of the military and the police. Can you explain to us what Martic would have had to take up with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republika Srpska part and not the newly created part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So are you saying that in order for your responsibilities to be shifted from the military structures to the police structures, Martic would have had to make that request directly to President Karadzic? Is that how I'm to understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood it correctly. If my chief is not authorised, Colonel Petar Jakovljevic, to agree to that, because it was planned that I would move up to a higher duty to be a police general. This calling was low-ranking by establishment, so I was supposed to go to the main administration, the Security Administration of Republika Srpska in Han Pijesak to General Tolimir and Salapura as an analyst.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You've had a very interesting career path, it seems to me. You were a senior-level police officer before the war. Then you were a military intelligence operative. And then you went back to the police. Did you have to resign from the military, demobilise, in order to take up the police post again?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to explain. The Law on the Military provides for the armed forces to be represented by the army and the police; whereas, in war time the police is subordinated to the army. It becomes part of specific military formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So, in other words, you could have a position and an affiliation with both the police and the military at the same time in a context of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could have worked for the police and for the army. But since this is professional work and it's employment, as an employee, according to the Law on Labour, I could be an employee of only one of those structures. It's another thing as how this work overlaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In practice -- I understand what you are saying. You are saying that you could only be an employee of one of those structures. In practice, could you carry out tasks for both of those structures simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could. But in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I did not do anything for the military structure. There was no need for that. I didn't want it, and they didn't ask for me either. One more remark. After I was wounded, my work capacity was reduced. I couldn't carry a backpack and a mortar, so I needed to work on administrative, material, technical kind of tasks; for example, interviews, criminal charges, that type of work. I have the status of a wounded -- or disabled veteran right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: One last question on your career. Who was your highest reporting officer, your highest superior, when you operated as a military intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zdravko Tolimir, who is currently detained by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what was the position he held at that time, that he was your superior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the main administration for security of the Army of Republika Srpska. And then there were some intermediate steps between us. But in the case of specific assignments, I would receive direct tasks from him personally. He was looking for a way to resolve my housing situation so that I would not have to leave the military, because my apartment in Croatia was confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Djukic. There are a number of individuals I'd like to ask you about based upon your experience in Bosanski Samac. These are people who you did not describe, at least not in depth, in your testimony so far. Could you tell us if you know Mile Beronja?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, after the replacement of Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, who was mentioned here, who was replaced when a lot of people were killed and my village of Cerik and my village -- and the village of Avramovina were torched. I believe that that was not done very well. On the 17th of June he helped me, but on 27th of August, his position was not that good. It's not a question of whether it was my village or not, but it was important because -- as a strategic point because of an important key road that was going through there, leading to other Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you mentioned the name of two villages. Could you please repeat the name, you said Dragomir Crni -- I think you said: "Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, who was mentioned here who was replaced when a lot of people were killed in my village of ... and the village of ... and we didn't catch the names of the villages." Could you repeat them, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Avramovina, Avramovina, and a hamlet called Grabov Gaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And then you said he helped me on 17th of June. Who were you referring to? Beronja or to Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It was not about the defence. I said that Djordjevic helped -- promised to help me. He sent a separate platoon to my village. There was a fierce attack on the 17th of June. The enemy was very numerous. I was with my younger son. We managed to throw back the enemy. And then another thing that I appreciate him for even more was that after the fall of Cerik, he issued an order that all military conscripts who were not 18 and who had not served their military term of duty had to leave the war zone. And that is how he saved my son from having to be in the war anymore, and he probably saved his life, too, because my older son was already disabled after the 23rd of March of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please restart, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness explained in response to his question [as interpreted] the number and the circumstances and the manner of the death of the people who were mentioned in one of the previous answers, and I don't see any of that in this answer in lines -- from line -- from 9 to 19, and perhaps it would be useful to clarify that so that we could clarify the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the last answer before you intervened?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it in the hands of Ms. Marcus whether she wants to have this clarified or not, because if he told us about it -- he certainly was only asked about whether it was Beronja or Djordjevic, and from the answer it's clear that it was Djordjevic and some additional information was given. I leave it in your hands, Ms. Marcus. Even stronger, I leave it in your hands for tomorrow. And if you think that relevant information, although not responsive to the question, Mr. Petrovic, then you may report this to the Chamber, and then -- or perhaps discuss it with Ms. Marcus first, because these are details apparently outside the scope of the question. Ms. Marcus, in view of your original estimate, what about two sessions for you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies. I do not think I will be able to finish in two sessions. My original estimate was three and a half hours, but Mr. Petrovic used three hours and 15 minutes, if I'm not mistaken. But with the additional evidence that was led that we didn't know of, plus the additional topics covered by Mr. Jordash, I was going to request a total of four hours. I can certainly try to reduce that to the extent possible, but I'm very sorry, I will not be able -- I do not think I'll be able to finish in two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider your response. But whatever happens, we'll adjourn for the day. Mr. Djukic, we would like to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Mr. Djukic, we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll continue tomorrow, Thursday, the 8th of March, in this same courtroom, II, at 9.00 in the morning. And I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
